status_reasoning: Reviewers state the conclusion that 'eQTMs are mostly independent of the mechanism involved in the repressive effect of DNA methylation on expression across genes' is 'currently poorly supported.' They note that partitioning eQTMs into only two bins (positive/negative) may mask important relationships, as 'most of the pos- and neg-eQTM effects are insignificant (around 0)' creating 'a sea of noise.' They require finer binning analysis to validate whether the negative correlation is genuine or 'an artifact of the binning.'

Reviewers raise two concerns about DMR associations with eQTMs and mQTLs. First, they note the relationship 'might be a byproduct of their relation with the average methylation' since 'the higher the average, the higher the variance,' requiring analysis of normalized differentiation values. Second, they state 'the additional biological conclusions are over-stretched and should be toned down,' indicating the interpretive claims (C4, C38) exceed what the data support.

Reviewers explicitly state 'The differential association of mQTLs to CGI and non-CGI promoters is intriguing and well supported.' While they request that 'analysis of pos- and neg-eQTMs should be repeated with finer binning,' they note the analysis 'is otherwise satisfactory,' indicating acceptance of the core findings about mQTL depletion in CGI promoters and enrichment in non-CGI promoters.

Reviewers characterize the claim about lack of methylation contribution to ASE as 'a strong assertion, but is also a negative result.' They express that 'it is hard to devise an appropriate control here' and explicitly 'urge the authors to remove this result, unless they can provide additional support,' indicating they do not accept the claim as currently supported.

Reviewers note that 'Figure 3C shows that there is a clear inflation in the resulting P-values' despite authors claiming to have controlled for artificial inflation. They state 'Without correcting for this, it is impossible to judge the number of significant relations' and advise using 'bootstrapping for some empirical correction' and correction 'for population structure and other confounders,' indicating the statistical validity of the interaction findings is questionable.

Reviewers raise concerns that 'the correction with AIC is based on theoretical considerations and hence might not compensate for the different degrees of freedom' among the three models. They note 'there is no evaluation of the significance of the resulting predicted models' which 'precludes the authors – and future readers – from following up on individual findings.' They require permutation testing to establish significance thresholds and discriminate significant from non-significant predictions before the causality model conclusions can be accepted.

Reviewers acknowledge this is 'an intriguing and important direction' but state 'it has to be done carefully.' They note 'it is not clear whether the reported P-values are corrected for the special characteristics of the data' and require 'a permutation test and deriving a corrected P-value' to evaluate statistical significance. They also state that 'in the absence of such follow up' biological experiments, 'the conclusions should be toned down significantly.'
